questions.stem: A 32-year-old female presents with pain and tenderness over the right clavicle. Physical examination reveals localized swelling and crepitus upon palpation. Radiological imaging shows a midshaft clavicle fracture. Which anatomical structure is most commonly affected in this type of fracture?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Middle third of the clavicle

 

The clavicle is commonly divided into three anatomical segments: the medial third, middle third, and lateral third. 

 

According to Allman orthopedic classifications, approximately 85% of fractures occur at the middle third of the clavicle, making this the most frequently affected area in clavicular fractures. This is due to the fact that the middle third is the weakest part of the bone and is subjected to the most stress during physical trauma. 

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Sternoclavicular joint: This joint is located at the medial end of the clavicle, where it articulates with the sternum. Fractures in the midshaft region of the clavicle are distant from this joint, so it is typically not involved in midshaft fractures. The sternoclavicular joint is involved more with injuries affecting the medial third of the clavicle.

 

Option B.  Acromioclavicular joint: This joint is located at the lateral end of the clavicle, where the clavicle meets the acromion of the scapula. It is also distant from the midshaft of the clavicle and is usually involved in lateral third clavicle injuries, rather than midshaft fractures.

 

Option C. Coracoclavicular ligaments: These ligaments stabilize the clavicle by connecting it to the coracoid process of the scapula. While these ligaments may be affected in fractures of the lateral third of the clavicle, they are typically not involved in midshaft fractures.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The middle third of the clavicle is the most common site for clavicle fractures, accounting for approximately 85% of cases. This is a key anatomical fact that should be remembered when dealing with trauma to the clavicular region.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following statements regarding the marked structure is accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: It is example of pressure epiphysis.

options.label: B
options.text: It gives attachment to long head of humerus and coracobrachialis.

options.label: C
options.text: It is palpable in delto-pectoral groove.

options.label: D
options.text: It is not palpable in infraclavicular fossa even in thin built persons.

questions.answerText: It is palpable in delto-pectoral groove.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) It is palpable in delto-pectoral groove

 

The coracoid process of the scapula is the marked structure in this question. It is a bony prominence that serves as an attachment site for several muscles, including the short head of the biceps brachii and the coracobrachialis. 

 

The coracoid process can be palpated in the delto-pectoral groove, which is the anatomical space between the deltoid and pectoralis major muscles. This is an important clinical landmark used during examinations to locate the coracoid process, especially in patients with shoulder injuries.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. It is example of pressure epiphysis: This is incorrect because the coracoid process is an example of an atavistic epiphysis, meaning it was once a separate bone during development but later fused with the scapula. A pressure epiphysis, on the other hand, refers to areas of bone subjected to pressure during growth, such as the head of the humerus.

 

Option B.  It gives attachment to long head of humerus and coracobrachialis: This is incorrect. The coracoid process provides attachment to the short head of the biceps brachii and coracobrachialis muscles, not the long head of the biceps or the humerus.

 

Option D. It is not palpable in infraclavicular fossa even in thin built persons: This statement is incorrect. The coracoid process is generally palpable in the infraclavicular fossa, especially in individuals with a thin build. It is located below the lateral third of the clavicle and can be palpated easily.

 

Educational Objective:

questions.stem: Which of the following clinical statements are true? A. Congenital absence of pectoralis major is known as Poland syndrome.B. Due to damage of Bell’s nerve (long thoracic nerve), winging of scapula occurs.C. Congenital high scapula is also known as Sprengel's deformity.D. In Cleidocranial dysostosis, clavicle is absent and shoulders can be approximated.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) A, B, C, D

 

A. Poland syndrome is a congenital condition where there is an absence or underdevelopment of the pectoralis major muscle on one side of the body, leading to visible deformity is a classical feature of Poland syndrome.

 

 

B.  Winging of the scapula occurs due to damage to the long thoracic nerve (also known as Bell’s nerve). This nerve supplies the serratus anterior muscle, which stabilizes the scapula. When the nerve is damaged, the scapula protrudes, leading to a winging appearance.

 

 

C. Congenital high scapula is indeed known as Sprengel's deformity. It is a rare congenital disorder where one of the scapulae is positioned higher than the other, often leading to a reduced range of motion in the shoulder.

 

 

D. Cleidocranial dysostosis is a genetic disorder characterized by absent or underdeveloped clavicles, which allows the shoulders to be approximated or brought closer together, a unique feature of this condition.

 

 

Educational Objective:

 

Poland syndrome involves underdevelopment of the pectoralis major, causing noticeable asymmetry. Winging of the scapula results from long thoracic nerve damage, leading to protrusion. Sprengel's deformity and cleidocranial dysostosis present with distinctive skeletal abnormalities that affect shoulder structure and mobility.

questions.stemHtml: A 42-year-old software engineer presents to the clinic complaining of chronic neck pain and stiffness. The pain is localized on the back and side of the neck and sometimes radiates to the shoulder. The patient reports that the pain worsens after long periods of working on the computer. Physical examination reveals tenderness and tightness in the upper neck region. Pain is particularly exacerbated by rotating the head to the opposite side and tilting it downwards. Marked muscle is most likely involved in this patient's condition. What is the nerve supply of this muscle?

options.label: C
options.text: From the dorsal rami of C1

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Dorsal scapular nerve

 

The levator scapulae is the muscle most likely involved in this patient's symptoms of neck pain and stiffness, especially given the history of posture-related strain and the physical exam findings of pain upon neck rotation and tilting. The levator scapulae elevates the scapula and rotates the neck. It is innervated by the dorsal scapular nerve (C5), which also innervates the rhomboid muscles. This nerve originates from the brachial plexus and is responsible for the motor function of these muscles, which can become tight or strained in individuals with poor posture, especially those who work long hours at a computer.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B.  Suprascapular nerve: The suprascapular nerve supplies the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles, which are primarily involved in abduction and external rotation of the arm. This nerve is unrelated to the levator scapulae and its functions, making it an incorrect option.

 

Option C. From the dorsal rami of C1: The dorsal rami of C1, also known as the suboccipital nerve, innervates muscles of the suboccipital triangle, including the rectus capitis posterior and obliquus capitis muscles. These muscles are primarily responsible for movements of the head, not scapular elevation, so this is incorrect for the levator scapulae.

 

Option D. Subscapular nerve: The subscapular nerve innervates the subscapularis muscle, part of the rotator cuff. This muscle is responsible for internal rotation of the shoulder joint and is not involved in scapular elevation or neck movement. Therefore, it is not relevant to this case.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The levator scapulae muscle, involved in neck elevation and movement, is innervated by the dorsal scapular nerve (C5), and its strain is often associated with neck pain and stiffness due to poor posture or overuse.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old male with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia presents to the emergency department with acute onset of severe chest pain radiating to the right arm, which started while he was gardening. An ECG reveals ST-segment elevation in the inferior leads. Coronary angiography is likely to show occlusion of the right coronary artery. All of the following are true about this artery except:

options.label: A
options.text: Its diameter is less than the left coronary artery

options.label: B
options.text: It arises from the anterior aortic sinus

options.label: C
options.text: It gives rise to the circumflex coronary branch

options.label: D
options.text: Right conus artery is its first branch

questions.answerText: It gives rise to the circumflex coronary branch
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) It gives rise to circumflex coronary branch

 

The right coronary artery (RCA) is responsible for supplying blood to the right atrium, right ventricle, and parts of the conduction system of the heart. It arises from the anterior aortic sinus, which is the correct origin of this artery. The right conus artery, which supplies the conus arteriosus (part of the right ventricle outflow tract), is the first branch of the RCA.

 

The RCA generally has a smaller diameter than the left coronary artery (LCA), as the LCA supplies a larger portion of the heart, including the left ventricle.

 

The incorrect statement is option C, as the circumflex branch is actually a part of the LCA, not the RCA. The circumflex artery branches off from the left coronary artery and supplies the lateral and posterior walls of the left ventricle.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Its diameter is less than the left coronary artery: This is correct. The RCA typically has a smaller diameter compared to the LCA, which supplies a larger portion of the heart.

 

Option. B.  It arises from the anterior aortic sinus: This is correct. The RCA originates from the anterior aortic sinus of the ascending aorta.

 

Option. D. Right conus artery is its first branch: This is correct. The right conus artery, which supplies the conus arteriosus, is indeed the first branch of the RCA.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The right coronary artery (RCA) does not give rise to the circumflex coronary branch, which is a branch of the left coronary artery (LCA). Understanding the branching of the coronary arteries is critical in diagnosing coronary artery disease.

questions.stem: Which of these is not a type of synovial joint?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Symphysis pubis

 

The symphysis pubis is classified as a secondary cartilaginous joint (also known as an amphiarthrosis), not a synovial joint. In this type of joint, the bones are united by fibrocartilage, allowing for limited movement. In the case of the symphysis pubis, the fibrocartilage is located between the two pubic bones.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Costotransverse joint: This is a plane synovial joint between the tubercle of the rib and the transverse process of the vertebra, allowing for slight gliding movements, especially during respiration.

 

Option B.  Costovertebral joint: The costovertebral joint is a plane synovial joint formed between the head of the rib and the bodies of the thoracic vertebrae. Like the costotransverse joint, it contributes to rib movements during breathing.

 

Option C. Radiocarpal joint: The radiocarpal joint, commonly known as the wrist joint, is a synovial joint (ellipsoid type), which allows for flexion, extension, abduction, and adduction of the hand.

 

Educational Objective:

questions.stem: Which among the following is incorrect regarding Sibson's fascia?

options.label: A
options.text: Attached to the inner border of 2nd rib

questions.answerText: Attached to the inner border of 2nd rib
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Attached to the inner border of 2nd rib

 

Sibson's fascia, also known as the suprapleural membrane, is a dense fascial layer that covers the apex of the lung and acts as a barrier between the neck and the thoracic cavity. It is attached to the inner border of the 1st rib, not the 2nd rib, This fascial structure provides protection for vital structures, such as the subclavian artery and vein, which pass above it.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B.  Covers apical part of lung: This is correct. Sibson's fascia extends over the apex of the lung, providing protection and structure to the area.

 

Option C. Part of scalenus minimus muscle: This is correct. Sibson's fascia is often considered a derivative of the scalenus minimus muscle, a small muscle that may be present in some individuals and is involved in respiration.

 

Option D. Vessels pass above the fascia: This is correct. The subclavian artery and vein pass above Sibson's fascia, confirming the relationship of the fascia to these major vessels.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Sibson's fascia is attached to the inner border of the 1st rib, covers the apex of the lung, and plays a role in protecting the structures in the thoracic inlet, with vessels such as the subclavian artery and vein passing above it .

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with sudden severe chest pain. He has a history of hypertension, and you suspect aortic dissection. An urgent CT scan shows a widened aorta with a false lumen but no obvious signs of rupture. You note to your consultant that the dissection extends to the level of the aortic opening of the diaphragm and express your concern about possible damage to all the structures that pass through the aortic opening of the diaphragm. These structures include all of the following except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Vagal trunk

 

This is incorrect. The vagal trunk passes through the esophageal hiatus at the level of T10, not the aortic opening.

 

The aortic hiatus of the diaphragm is the opening through which certain structures pass between the thoracic and abdominal cavities. The main structures passing through this hiatus are the aorta, azygous vein, and the thoracic duct. The vagal trunk, however, does not pass through the aortic hiatus. Instead, it passes through the esophageal hiatus at the level of T10, along with the esophagus.

 

The aorta passes through the aortic opening at the level of T12.

 

The thoracic duct and azygous vein accompany the aorta through the aortic opening, making these structures correctly listed.

 

The vagal trunk, on the other hand, passes through the esophageal hiatus, not the aortic hiatus, which makes option D the incorrect answer.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Aorta: This is correct. The aorta passes through the aortic hiatus at the level of T12.

 

Option B.  Azygous vein: This is correct. The azygous vein passes through the aortic hiatus along with the aorta and the thoracic duct.

 

Option C. Thoracic duct: This is correct. The thoracic duct, which is the main lymphatic vessel, passes through the aortic opening of the diaphragm.

 

Educational Objective:

questions.stemHtml: What is the function of the muscle marked in the image below, at the metacarpophalangeal joint?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Flexion

 

The lumbrical muscles, which are likely the muscles marked in this question, play a significant role at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints. They originate from the tendons of the flexor digitorum profundus and insert into the extensor expansion on the dorsal side of the fingers. The primary function of the lumbricals at the MCP joints is flexion. Additionally, they extend the interphalangeal joints. This unique combination of actions allows for precise control during hand movements, such as gripping objects and maintaining dexterity.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B.  Extension: Extension at the metacarpophalangeal joints is not the primary function of the lumbricals. Instead, these muscles cause extension at the interphalangeal joints, helping with fine motor tasks.

 

Option C. Adduction: Adduction at the MCP joint is performed by the palmar interossei muscles, not the lumbricals. The lumbricals are involved in flexion, not adduction.

 

Option D. Abduction: Abduction at the MCP joint is primarily controlled by the dorsal interossei muscles, not the lumbricals. Thus, the lumbricals are not responsible for abduction of the fingers.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The lumbrical muscles perform flexion at the metacarpophalangeal joints and extension at the interphalangeal joints, allowing for refined and precise hand movements .

questions.stem: Following surgery for varicose veins, the patient is experiencing a complaint of sensory loss in the medial area of the leg and foot. Which of the following nerves is the most probable site of injury?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Saphenous nerve

 

The saphenous nerve is a branch of the femoral nerve that supplies sensory innervation to the medial side of the leg and foot. This nerve runs in close proximity to the great saphenous vein, making it susceptible to injury during varicose vein surgery. Damage to the saphenous nerve can result in numbness, tingling, or sensory loss in the medial region of the lower leg and foot, consistent with the symptoms described in this case.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Sural nerve: The sural nerve provides sensory innervation to the lateral side of the foot and lower leg. Since the patient’s sensory loss is on the medial side, involvement of the sural nerve is unlikely.

 

Option B.  Superficial peroneal nerve: The superficial peroneal nerve supplies sensory innervation to the dorsum of the foot and anterolateral aspect of the lower leg. Damage to this nerve would not explain the medial sensory loss.

 

Option. C. Deep peroneal nerve: The deep peroneal nerve supplies the first web space of the foot and is primarily involved in motor innervation to the muscles of the anterior compartment of the leg. It does not account for sensory loss in the medial region of the leg.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The saphenous nerve is vulnerable during varicose vein surgery and provides sensory innervation to the medial leg and foot

questions.stemHtml: Identify the cartilage shown below:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) White fibrocartilage

 

The image shows fibrocartilage/ White fibrocartilage, which is characterized by thick, red, wavy bundles of collagen fibers visible between the rows of chondrocytes. Fibrocartilage is a tough, dense type of cartilage that provides both rigidity and flexibility. The collagen bundles provide strength, making fibrocartilage the type of cartilage found in intervertebral discs and other areas where both flexibility and tensile strength are needed.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Non articular hyaline cartilage: This type of cartilage is found in the trachea, bronchi, and the nose. It appears more glassy with a smooth matrix lacking the thick collagen fibers seen in fibrocartilage.

 

Option B.  Articular hyaline cartilage: Articular hyaline cartilage covers the surfaces of bones in synovial joints. It lacks the wavy collagen bundles seen in fibrocartilage and instead has a smooth, glassy appearance with more evenly distributed chondrocytes.

 

Option C. Yellow cartilage: Also known as elastic cartilage, yellow cartilage contains elastic fibers, which give it flexibility. It is found in structures like the external ear and epiglottis, and its appearance is distinct from fibrocartilage due to the presence of elastic fibers.

 

Educational Objective:

 

White fibrocartilage is recognized by its thick, wavy bundles of collagen and is found in structures that require strength and the ability to withstand compression, such as intervertebral discs and pubic symphysis

questions.stem: During a yawn, a student experienced a jaw locking incident. Identify the muscle attached to the articular disc of the temporomandibular joint?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Lateral pterygoid

 

The lateral pterygoid muscle is the only muscle that attaches directly to the articular disc of the temporomandibular joint (TMJ). It plays an essential role in protracting the mandible (moving it forward) and is also involved in depressing the mandible (opening the mouth). During yawning, this muscle contracts, pulling the articular disc forward to allow for smooth movement of the mandible. If there is dysfunction or overactivity in the lateral pterygoid muscle, it can lead to jaw locking, as seen in this student's case.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B.  Temporalis: The temporalis muscle is primarily responsible for elevation and retraction of the mandible. It does not attach to the articular disc and is involved in closing the jaw.

 

Option C. Medial pterygoid: The medial pterygoid muscle assists in elevation and side-to-side movements of the mandible but does not attach to the articular disc.

 

Option D. Masseter: The masseter muscle is involved in elevation (closing the mouth) and plays a role in chewing, but it does not attach to the articular disc.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The lateral pterygoid is the only muscle that attaches to the articular disc of the TMJ and is responsible for protracting the mandible, which can lead to jaw locking if it malfunctions​

questions.stem: All of the following structures are derived from the aponeurosis of the external oblique muscle except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Linea semilunaris



The external oblique muscle is a major muscle of the anterior abdominal wall, and its aponeurosis gives rise to several important anatomical structures. The aponeurosis of the external oblique forms the Inguinal ligament, Pectineal ligament, and the Lacunar ligament. These are important derivatives of this muscle’s aponeurosis.

 

The Inguinal ligament runs from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the pubic tubercle and is formed by the lower border of the aponeurosis.

 

The Lacunar ligament is a reflection of fibers of the inguinal ligament that form a small, triangular ligament connecting to the pubis.

 

The Pectineal ligament is a continuation of the Lacunar ligament along the pectineal line of the pubis.

 

However, the Linea semilunaris is not derived from the external oblique aponeurosis. It is a curved tendinous line that marks the lateral border of the rectus abdominis muscle, and while it is part of the anatomy of the abdominal wall, it is not a direct continuation of the external oblique aponeurosis.

 

Other Options:


Option A. Pectineal ligament: This is derived from the external oblique aponeurosis as a continuation of the inguinal and lacunar ligaments.
 

Option B.  Inguinal ligament: It is formed directly by the aponeurosis of the external oblique and serves as a significant landmark in the inguinal region.


Option C. Lacunar ligament: This ligament is also a derivative of the external oblique aponeurosis, forming a connection between the inguinal ligament and the pubis.

 

Educational Objective:

questions.stemHtml: Identify the marked cell from the given histological image of the cerebellum:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Purkinje cells

 

The marked cell in the given histological image is a Purkinje cell. Purkinje cells are large, flask-shaped neurons located in the Purkinje layer of the cerebellum, sandwiched between the molecular and granular layers. These cells are easily identifiable due to their distinctive shape and size. They possess extensive dendritic arborizations that extend into the molecular layer, which can be visualized in histological slides.

 

Purkinje cells play a crucial role in the motor coordination of the body. They are the sole output neurons of the cerebellar cortex and send inhibitory signals to the deep cerebellar nuclei, thus regulating the motor function. In the histological context of the cerebellum, these cells are among the largest and most prominent.

 

 

Other Options:
Option B.  Basket cells: These smaller inhibitory interneurons are found in the molecular layer of the cerebellum and are not as large or distinct as Purkinje cells.
Option C. Golgi cells: Golgi cells are found in the granular layer of the cerebellum. They are smaller than Purkinje cells and function as inhibitory interneurons, synapsing onto granule cells.
Option D. Granule cells: Granule cells are the smallest and most numerous neurons in the cerebellum, located in the granular layer. They are significantly smaller than Purkinje cells

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a projection from a bone surface?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Trabeculae


Trabeculae are not considered projections from a bone surface. Trabeculae refer to the small, often lattice-like, internal structures found in spongy (cancellous) bone. They are the structural components within the bone that form the framework of the spongy bone, providing support from within rather than projecting from the surface.

 

In contrast, the Trochanter, Tubercle, and Tuberosity are all types of bone projections where muscles, tendons, or ligaments attach. These projections help in the movement of muscles and are found on various bones like the femur (trochanter), humerus (tubercle), and other long bones.

 

 

Educational Objective:


Trabeculae are internal structures in spongy bone, not surface projections, while trochanter, tubercle, and tuberosity are surface projections involved in muscle and ligament attachment.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old male patient was admitted with complaints of acute pain in the right shoulder of three-days duration associated with swelling, and he also had difficulty using his right shoulder. Pain was sudden in onset, continuous, and moderate to severe I n intensity, aggravated by activity. He also experienced severe night and rest pain. The patient had a history of intramuscular injection of iron in the right deltoid region 2 weeks prior. MRI scan of the right shoulder revealed pyomyositis of the posterior belly of the right deltoid muscle with central abscess formation. Which among the following is NOT a possible complication that can be expected in this case if untreated?

options.label: A
options.text: Loss of sensation on the lower lateral aspect of the arm

options.label: C
options.text: Weak flexion of the arm at the shoulder joint

options.label: D
options.text: Inability to extend the arm at the shoulder joint

questions.answerText: Loss of sensation on the lower lateral aspect of the arm
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Loss of sensation on the lower lateral aspect of the arm


The deltoid muscle, supplied by the axillary nerve, plays a key role in shoulder movements, specifically in abduction, flexion, and extension of the arm. In this patient, an MRI has confirmed pyomyositis involving the posterior belly of the right deltoid muscle, which is consistent with the inability to move the shoulder properly.

 

The axillary nerve innervates the deltoid and teres minor muscles and provides sensory innervation to the skin covering the upper lateral part of the arm (the regimental badge area).

 

If the axillary nerve is compromised due to the abscess or subsequent inflammation, there can be inability to abduct the arm beyond 90 degrees, weak flexion (due to anterior deltoid involvement), and inability to extend the arm at the shoulder joint (due to posterior deltoid involvement).

 

However, loss of sensation on the lower lateral aspect of the arm would not occur, as this region is not supplied by the axillary nerve but rather by other cutaneous nerves.

 

Other Options:


Option B. Inability to abduct the shoulder: The deltoid muscle, primarily the middle fibers, is responsible for abduction of the arm up to 90 degrees. With involvement of the deltoid due to the abscess, abduction is expected to be impaired.


Option C. Weak flexion of the arm at the shoulder joint: The anterior fibers of the deltoid muscle are involved in flexion. Involvement of the deltoid due to the abscess would likely result in weak flexion of the arm.
 

Option D. Inability to extend the arm at the shoulder joint: The posterior fibers of the deltoid muscle are responsible for extension. If these fibers are involved, extension would be compromised.

 

Educational Objective:


In pyomyositis affecting the deltoid muscle, the patient may exhibit difficulties in abduction, flexion, and extension of the shoulder due to the involvement of different fibers of the deltoid, but loss of sensation in the lower lateral aspect of the arm is not expected, as this area is not innervated by the axillary nerve.

questions.stemHtml: Injury to the nerve that lies medially to the structure pointed will result in:

options.label: A
options.text: Loss of taste sensation from anterior 2/3 tongue

options.label: B
options.text: Loss of taste sensation from posterior 1/3 tongue

options.label: C
options.text: Loss of general sensation from anterior 2/3 tongue

options.label: D
options.text: Loss of taste sensation from posterior most part of tongue

questions.answerText: Loss of taste sensation from anterior 2/3 tongue
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Loss of taste sensation from anterior 2/3 tongue

 

The nerve that lies medially to the structure pointed in the image is the chorda tympani, which is a branch of the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII). This nerve is responsible for providing taste sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. If this nerve is injured, the patient would lose the ability to perceive taste in this portion of the tongue.

 

The chorda tympani courses medially to the spine of the sphenoid and enters the infratemporal fossa, where it joins the lingual nerve (a branch of the mandibular nerve) to supply the taste fibers to the anterior 2/3 of the tongue.

 

Other Options:


Option B. Loss of taste sensation from posterior 1/3 tongue: This function is provided by the glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX), not the chorda tympani, so this option is incorrect.
 

Option C. Loss of general sensation from anterior 2/3 tongue: General sensation (not taste) from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is provided by the lingual nerve, a branch of the mandibular nerve (cranial nerve V3), and is not affected by an injury to the chorda tympani.
 

Option D. Loss of taste sensation from posterior most part of tongue: The vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) provides taste sensation to the posterior most part of the tongue, not the chorda tympani.

 

Educational Objective:


Injury to the chorda tympani results in the loss of taste sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.

questions.stemHtml: A patient presents with a unilateral throbbing headache, photophobia, and excessive lacrimation. He also complains of hemifacial pain on clenching of teeth. On examination, pupillary reflex, light reflex, and accommodation reflex are normal. Which of the following marked nerves is involved in the below scenario?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) C. 3


The symptoms described—unilateral throbbing headache, photophobia, excessive lacrimation, and hemifacial pain on clenching of teeth—are indicative of trigeminal neuralgia. The trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V) is responsible for sensation in the face and motor functions such as biting and chewing. Specifically, V2 (maxillary division) and V3 (mandibular division) of the trigeminal nerve are often implicated in facial pain and discomfort.

 

The third marked nerve (3) corresponds to the trigeminal nerve (V) in this diagram, particularly its divisions which are involved in sensory and motor functions in the facial and jaw regions.

 

 

Other Options:


Option A. 1: This nerve is likely related to cranial nerve I (olfactory nerve), which is involved in smell sensation, not facial pain.
 

Option B. 2: This represents cranial nerve II (optic nerve), responsible for vision. There is no evidence in the scenario of vision problems, ruling out this option.
 

Option D. 4: This is cranial nerve IV (trochlear nerve), which controls the superior oblique muscle of the eye and is not involved in the described symptoms.

 

Educational Objective:


Trigeminal neuralgia affects the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V), causing facial pain and sensory issues, often triggered by simple actions like clenching teeth.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the papillae from the given histological section:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Circumvallate

 

Circumvallate papillae are large, circular papillae located towards the back of the tongue. They are characterized by their circular structure with a surrounding trench,. These papillae contain numerous taste buds, particularly located in the trenches. They are important for taste sensation and are easily identifiable in histological sections due to their size and distinct trench appearance. The circumvallate papillae also have a unique arrangement that forms a V-shape on the posterior tongue.

 

 

Other Options:


Option A. Fungiform: These papillae are smaller and mushroom-shaped, scattered across the surface of the tongue. They are not characterized by the trenches seen in circumvallate papillae.
 

Option C. Filiform: These are thread-like papillae found on the surface of the tongue. They are keratinized and do not contain taste buds, and they present with a pointed appearance in histological sections.
 

Option D. Foliate: These papillae have a leaf-like appearance with parallel ridges on the lateral sides of the tongue. They are more prominent in some animals and are rudimentary in humans.

 

Educational Objective:
 

Circumvallate papillae are large, circular structures with surrounding trenches, located at the back of the tongue, and they are heavily involved in taste sensation.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes the movements known as pronation and supination?

options.label: A
options.text: The flexing of the arm with respect to the forearm around the elbow

options.label: B
options.text: The elevation of the foot to the medial and lateral directions

options.label: C
options.text: The twisting of the wrist while the elbow is held motionless

options.label: D
options.text: The rotation at the shoulder that causes the arm to describe a cone shape

questions.answerText: The twisting of the wrist while the elbow is held motionless
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) The twisting of the wrist while the elbow is held motionless


Pronation and supination refer to rotational movements at the forearm that involve the twisting of the wrist. Pronation involves turning the palm of the hand downward or posteriorly, while supination turns the palm upward or anteriorly. These movements occur at the superior and inferior radioulnar joints. During this action, the elbow remains stable and motionless while the radius rotates around the ulna, causing the hand to twist into the pronated or supinated position.

 

Other Options:


Option A. The flexing of the arm with respect to the forearm around the elbow: This describes flexion, not pronation or supination, which occur at the forearm, not the elbow joint.
 

Option B. The elevation of the foot to the medial and lateral directions: This describes inversion and eversion of the foot, movements that occur at the ankle joint.
 

Option D. The rotation at the shoulder that causes the arm to describe a cone shape: This is circumduction, a movement that occurs at ball-and-socket joints like the shoulder, but it is not related to pronation and supination.

 

Educational Objective:


Pronation and supination are rotational movements of the forearm, where the radius rotates around the ulna, and they primarily involve twisting the wrist while the elbow remains motionless.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man presents to the clinic with complaints of weakness in his right arm after using crutches for six weeks due to a leg fracture. He mentions that the crutches were possibly too tall for him, as they pressed hard into his armpit. On examination, there is a notable deficit in the extension of his wrist and fingers, and he has difficulty with thumb abduction. His sense of touch is diminished over the posterior aspect of his arm and forearm and the dorsum of his hand. Given the distribution of his symptoms, which structure is most likely to be affected by the prolonged use of crutches?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Posterior cord


The patient's symptoms of wrist and finger extension weakness, difficulty with thumb abduction, and sensory loss over the posterior arm and forearm, as well as the dorsum of the hand, strongly indicate an injury to the radial nerve, which is derived from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus. This condition, often termed "crutch palsy," occurs due to prolonged pressure on the axilla from improper use of crutches, leading to compression of the radial nerve.

 

The radial nerve supplies the muscles responsible for wrist and finger extension (extensor muscles of the forearm) and sensation over the posterior aspect of the arm, forearm, and dorsum of the hand. The weakness in wrist extension results in wrist drop, a classic sign of radial nerve injury. The posterior cord gives rise to the radial and axillary nerves, both of which are vulnerable to compression in the axilla due to improper crutch use.

 

Branches of Brachial Nerve 

 

 

Other Options:


Option B. Lateral cord: This cord gives rise to nerves such as the musculocutaneous and a portion of the median nerve, which do not innervate the posterior arm and forearm or control wrist extension.
 

Option C. Medial cord: This cord primarily supplies the ulnar nerve, which innervates the intrinsic muscles of the hand, but not the muscles responsible for wrist or finger extension.
 

Option D. Upper trunk: The upper trunk of the brachial plexus gives rise to nerves that innervate the shoulder muscles and parts of the arm, but it does not specifically contribute to the radial nerve or result in wrist drop when injured.

 

Educational Objective:


Injury to the posterior cord of the brachial plexus, often caused by improper crutch use, can lead to radial nerve compression, resulting in wrist drop and sensory loss over the posterior arm, forearm, and hand.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old auto driver was attacked by a mob over a family quarrel and received a stab wound at the front of the neck. He was rushed to the emergency department. The knife entrance wound was located on the right side of the neck just lateral to the tip of the greater cornu of the hyoid bone. During the physical examination, the patient was asked to protrude his tongue, which deviated to the right. Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding the physical signs in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Paralysis of the right genioglossus muscle permitted the left genioglossus to pull the tongue forward and turned the tip to the right side

options.label: B
options.text: Genioglossus originates from the lower genial tubercles of the mandible

options.label: C
options.text: The hypoglossal nerve descends in the neck between the internal carotid artery and the internal jugular vein

options.label: D
options.text: At about the level of the tip of the greater cornu of the hyoid bone, the hypoglossal nerve turns forward and crosses the internal and external carotid arteries and the lingual artery to enter the tongue

questions.answerText: Genioglossus originates from the lower genial tubercles of the mandible
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Genioglossus originates from the lower genial tubercles of the mandible


Patient sustained a wound in the neck near the hypoglossal nerve, which controls the movement of the tongue. The paralysis of the right genioglossus muscle led to the deviation of the tongue to the right side due to the unopposed action of the left genioglossus muscle, pulling the tongue toward the affected side during protrusion. This indicates damage to the hypoglossal nerve (cranial nerve XII) on the right side.

 

The genioglossus muscle is responsible for protruding the tongue, and it originates from the upper genial tubercles (not the lower) of the mandible, The lower genial tubercles give rise to the geniohyoid muscle, which is involved in other movements of the hyoid bone.

 

The hypoglossal nerve passes between the internal carotid artery and the internal jugular vein before turning forward at the level of the greater cornu of the hyoid bone, where it crosses the internal and external carotid arteries and the lingual artery to enter the tongue.

 

Other Options:
 

Option A. Paralysis of the right genioglossus muscle permitted the left genioglossus to pull the tongue forward and turn the tip to the right side: This statement is correct as the tongue deviates toward the paralyzed side due to the action of the opposing genioglossus.
 

Option C. The hypoglossal nerve descends in the neck between the internal carotid artery and the internal jugular vein: This is a correct anatomical description of the course of the hypoglossal nerve.
 

Option D. At about the level of the tip of the greater cornu of the hyoid bone, the hypoglossal nerve turns forward and crosses the internal and external carotid arteries and the lingual artery to enter the tongue: This statement is also correct, as it accurately describes the path of the hypoglossal nerve.

 

Educational Objective:


The genioglossus muscle originates from the upper genial tubercles of the mandible, and paralysis of one side causes the tongue to deviate toward the paralyzed side during protrusion.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy was brought to the hospital with multiple fractures of the humerus secondary to a fall from height. On examination, there is difficulty in flexion of the elbow and supination of the forearm, and associated loss of sensation over the lateral aspect of the forearm. Which nerve is most likely to be injured?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Musculocutaneous nerve


The musculocutaneous nerve is responsible for innervating the muscles that flex the elbow (such as the biceps brachii and brachialis muscles) and assists in the supination of the forearm. In addition, the nerve provides sensory innervation to the lateral aspect of the forearm via the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm , symptoms, including weakness in elbow flexion and forearm supination along with sensory loss over the lateral forearm, are consistent with an injury to the musculocutaneous nerve.

 

The fracture of the humerus likely caused damage to this nerve, affecting both motor and sensory functions, particularly the biceps brachii, which is a powerful supinator of the forearm and a major flexor of the elbow.

 

Other Options:


Option A. Median nerve: The median nerve mainly supplies the anterior compartment of the forearm and is involved in pronation of the forearm, not supination or elbow flexion.
 

Option B. Radial nerve: Although the radial nerve supplies some extensors of the arm and forearm, it is not primarily responsible for flexion of the elbow or supination.
 

Option D. Ulnar nerve: The ulnar nerve supplies muscles in the hand and does not significantly affect elbow flexion or forearm supination.

 

Educational Objective:


Injury to the musculocutaneous nerve leads to weakness in elbow flexion, difficulty in forearm supination, and sensory loss over the lateral forearm, as seen in cases involving humeral fractures.

questions.stemHtml: The patient presented with exacerbated chronic lower back pain in the sacral region, radiating to the back of the left leg, causing intense throbbing and burning pain behind the knee. The pain worsened with bending forward or reaching out. The patient had a history of a congenital back condition and a previous lumbar vertebra fracture due to an accident. An MRI conducted two months earlier showed L1 degeneration, disc degeneration, and disc protrusion at the S1 level. Despite being prescribed strong non-steroidal pain medication, the pain relief was insufficient, and the medication caused drowsiness. The patient sought alternative treatment with InterX therapy, which targeted the entire lumbar-sacral zone, dermatomes L1/L2, L4, L5, S1–S3, and the left and right buttocks, as well as the left back of the knee. After two and a half weeks of therapy, the patient reported complete pain relief, discontinued pain medication, and began core exercises to stabilize the lumbar spine. The patient was advised to limit driving, prolonged sitting, rest, follow a good diet, and perform gentle stretching exercises. A six-month follow-up confirmed that the patient remained pain-free, was actively working, and traveling. All of the following anatomical statements are true about this case except?

options.label: A
options.text: A & D arise from the same bony point

options.label: B
options.text: C runs between a vein and a nerve

options.label: C
options.text: B is affected in this case, causing all symptoms

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Arteria nervi ischiadici supplies B
 


In this case, the patient suffered from chronic lower back pain with sciatic involvement, as indicated by the pain radiating down the left leg and behind the knee. The nerve likely involved is the sciatic nerve (B), which is affected due to the disc degeneration and protrusion at the S1 level. This nerve is responsible for the symptoms described, including pain and dysfunction in the lower extremity.

 

Arteria nervi ischiadici supplies B: This statement is incorrect. The sciatic nerve is not primarily supplied by the Arteria nervi ischiadici; it is more accurately supplied by branches of the internal iliac artery.

 

Other Options

 

Option A. A & D arise from the same bony point: This is a correct statement as the muscles shown arise from the same bony origin.

 

A is semimembranosus muscle

 

D is semitendinosus muscle

 

Both of these structures originate from ischial tuberosity.
 

 

Option B.  C runs between a vein and a nerve: This is true for the indicated structure.

 

C is a popliteal artery which is travelling from the anterior compartment of the thigh to the posterior compartment.

 

Option C. B is affected in this case, causing all symptoms: The sciatic nerve (B) is responsible for the symptoms experienced by the patient, including radiating pain and nerve dysfunction.

 

 

Educational Objective:
 

In cases of sciatic nerve involvement due to lumbar disc degeneration or protrusion, the nerve responsible for the pain is typically the sciatic nerve, but it is not supplied by the Arteria nervi ischiadici.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old construction worker presents to the emergency department following a workplace accident. He reports a fall from a height, landing awkwardly on his right leg. The patient complains of severe pain and weakness in the lower limb, particularly on the lateral side of his right leg. On examination, there is noticeable foot drop with decreased sensation over the dorsum of the foot and the lateral leg. Which nerve injury is most likely responsible for the observed symptoms of foot drop and sensory deficit in this patient's right lower limb?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Common peroneal nerve


The common peroneal nerve (also known as the common fibular nerve) is the most likely nerve to be injured in this case. This nerve wraps around the head of the fibula and is particularly vulnerable to trauma, especially in cases of direct impact or awkward landings. Damage to the common peroneal nerve can result in foot drop, where the patient cannot dorsiflex the foot. This leads to difficulty lifting the front part of the foot, resulting in a "slapping" gait. Additionally, the common peroneal nerve supplies sensation to the lateral side of the leg and the dorsum of the foot, which matches the sensory deficits observed in the patient.

 

Remember - Foot drop - Injury of CPN > DPN > SCIATIC NERVE

 

Other Options:


Option B. Femoral nerve: This nerve innervates the muscles responsible for hip flexion and knee extension. An injury to the femoral nerve would not result in foot drop or sensory loss in the areas described.
 

Option C. Sciatic nerve: While the sciatic nerve does give rise to the common peroneal and tibial nerves, damage to the sciatic nerve would typically present with more extensive motor and sensory deficits involving the posterior thigh, not just foot drop and isolated sensory loss on the dorsum of the foot.
 

Option D. Tibial nerve: The tibial nerve innervates the muscles of the posterior compartment of the leg and the plantar muscles of the foot. An injury to the tibial nerve would cause deficits in plantarflexion and sensation on the sole of the foot, not foot drop or loss of sensation on the dorsum of the foot.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Injury to the common peroneal nerve is the most common cause of foot drop and results in sensory deficits on the lateral side of the leg and dorsum of the foot.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male presents to the clinic with a history of progressive weakness in his right leg. He reports difficulty in climbing stairs and rising from a seated position. During examination, the patient demonstrates noticeable weakness in his right hip joint movement against resistance. Additionally, there is reduced ability to extend his right thigh while lying prone. Which nerve's involvement in supplying the chief extensor of the thigh at the hip joint might correspond to the observed weakness and limitations in this patient's right leg?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Inferior gluteal nerve


The inferior gluteal nerve supplies the gluteus maximus, which is the chief extensor of the thigh at the hip joint. This nerve arises from the sacral plexus and innervates the gluteus maximus, responsible for extending the hip, particularly during powerful movements such as climbing stairs or rising from a seated position. The weakness in hip extension and difficulty with these activities strongly indicates damage or dysfunction of the inferior gluteal nerve.

 

The patient's symptoms, such as weakness when climbing stairs and rising from a seated position, and reduced ability to extend the thigh, are characteristic signs of impaired gluteus maximus function due to inferior gluteal nerve involvement.

 

Other Options:


Option B. Superior gluteal nerve: This nerve supplies the gluteus medius and minimus muscles, which are responsible for hip abduction and medial rotation, not extension.


Option C. Sciatic nerve: While the sciatic nerve supplies many muscles in the posterior thigh, it is not primarily responsible for the extension of the hip.


Option D. Peroneal nerve: The peroneal (or fibular) nerve innervates muscles involved in dorsiflexion and eversion of the foot, not hip extension.

 

Educational Objective:


The inferior gluteal nerve innervates the gluteus maximus, the chief extensor of the thigh at the hip joint, and damage to this nerve results in weakness during hip extension activities like climbing stairs or rising from a seated position.

questions.stem: Which of the following are branches of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery? Superior gluteal arteryInferior gluteal arterySuperior vesical arteryMiddle rectal arteryInferior vesical arteryVaginal artery
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) 2, 3, 4, 5, 6

 

The anterior division of the internal iliac artery supplies various pelvic structures and gives rise to multiple branches. In this case, the correct branches from the anterior division include:

 

2.Inferior gluteal artery: This artery supplies the gluteal region and arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery.

 

3.Superior vesical artery: This artery supplies the bladder and originates from the anterior division.

 

4.Middle rectal artery: It supplies the rectum and is also a branch of the anterior division.

 

5. Inferior vesical artery: This artery, which supplies the lower part of the bladder, is another branch from the anterior division.

 

6.Vaginal artery: This artery supplies the vagina and is part of the anterior division.

 

 

Other Options

 

Option 1. The superior gluteal artery: is actually a branch of the posterior division of the internal iliac artery, which makes options A and D incorrect.

 

Educational Objective:
 

Branches of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery include the inferior gluteal, superior vesical, middle rectal, inferior vesical, and vaginal arteries. The superior gluteal artery comes from the posterior division.

questions.stem: A patient, Vinod, who has taken the first COVID vaccine comes for the second dose. A nurse noticed that the shoulder was flabby, flat, and asymmetrical. There was an associated loss of contour of the shoulder joint. Injury to which of the structures might have resulted and was avoidable?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Deltoid muscle


The symptoms of a flabby, flat, and asymmetrical shoulder with loss of contour indicate injury to the deltoid muscle. The deltoid is responsible for giving the shoulder its rounded contour and is crucial for abduction of the arm. Injury to this muscle, especially in cases like improper injection placement, can lead to muscle atrophy and a flattened shoulder appearance. Intramuscular injections should ideally avoid the region near the axillary nerve, which innervates the deltoid, to prevent such complications.

 

In this patient, the likely mechanism is a misapplied injection affecting the axillary nerve, leading to dysfunction of the deltoid muscle, resulting in the described symptoms.

 

Other Options:



Option A. Rotator cuff: The rotator cuff muscles stabilize the shoulder joint and help in arm movements but are not primarily responsible for the shoulder's contour. Injury here would result in specific shoulder movement issues but not a flabby appearance.

 

Option B. Posterior circumflex artery: While this artery supplies blood to the shoulder region, its injury would lead to vascular complications like bleeding or ischemia but not muscle atrophy or flabbiness.

 

Option C. Lateral cutaneous nerve of arm: This nerve provides sensation to the upper arm and does not play a role in maintaining the muscle bulk or shoulder contour.

 

Educational Objective:


The deltoid muscle is crucial for the rounded contour of the shoulder. Injury to the axillary nerve, which supplies the deltoid, can lead to atrophy, resulting in a flat, flabby, and asymmetrical shoulder.

questions.stemHtml: The marked structures in the image are a pair of small, round nuclei located on the undersurface of the brain. They form part of the limbic system and are involved in memory processing and recall. Damage to them is commonly associated with Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, typically seen in chronic alcoholics and characterized by confabulation, memory impairment, and ataxia. These structures receive signals from the hippocampus via the fornix and project to the anterior nucleus of the thalamus, playing a crucial role in the Papez circuit, which is important for emotional expression and memory consolidation. Fibers from the marked structure end in which of the following areas of the thalamus?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Anterior nucleus


The marked structures are the mammillary bodies, which are involved in memory processing and are part of the limbic system. The mammillary bodies are known to relay information from the hippocampus to the anterior nucleus of the thalamus via the mammillothalamic tract. This circuit is crucial for memory consolidation and emotional processing, which is part of the Papez circuit.

 

Damage to the mammillary bodies is often linked to Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, which is typically caused by chronic alcoholism and results in symptoms such as confabulation, memory impairment, and ataxia. The anterior nucleus of the thalamus is a significant relay station in this memory pathway, receiving inputs from the mammillary bodies and projecting to the cingulate gyrus.

 

Other Options:


Option A. Posterior nucleus: This nucleus is involved in different thalamic functions, particularly related to pain and temperature sensation, and is not connected to the mammillary bodies.
 

Option B. Reticular nucleus: The reticular nucleus of the thalamus is part of the reticular activating system, associated with consciousness and arousal, not memory processing.
 

Option D. Ventral lateral nucleus: This nucleus is involved in motor control and coordination, primarily receiving input from the cerebellum, rather than from the mammillary bodies.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Papez circuit - Impulses go from the anterior nucleus of thalamus → to cingulate gyrus (center  for satisfaction ) → hippocampus → mammillary body → finally to the anterior nucleus of

thalamus again.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old male presented with history of frequency, hesitancy, and urgency for urination. He was on medication of Tamsulosin and Finasteride combination. Now Trans Urethral Resection of Prostate (TURP) surgery was recommended by the physician. What is the volume of the prostate in normal adult males?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) 20 cc


The normal volume of the prostate in an adult male is 20 cc. This is a baseline measurement, and the prostate tends to increase in size with conditions such as benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) or prostate cancer, often necessitating interventions like TURP.

 

Medications such as Tamsulosin and Finasteride are commonly prescribed to manage symptoms of BPH by improving urine flow and reducing the size of the prostate.

 

Educational Objective:


The normal volume of the prostate in an adult male is approximately 20 cc, and enlargement beyond this can indicate conditions like BPH.

questions.stemHtml: Which structure from the options given below is supplied by the nerve that arises from the marked area in the image?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Risorius


The Risorius muscle is a muscle of facial expression that is supplied by the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII). The facial nerve arises from the pons and courses through the internal acoustic meatus, eventually emerging to supply the muscles responsible for facial movements, including the Risorius. This muscle pulls the angle of the mouth laterally, contributing to expressions like smiling.

 

The marked area in the image refers to the region of the brainstem where cranial nerves, including the facial nerve, arise, which is consistent with the innervation of the Risorius muscle.

 

Other Options:
 

Option A. Lateral rectus: This muscle is innervated by the abducens nerve (cranial nerve VI), which is responsible for abducting the eye, not facial expression.
 

Option B. Superior oblique: This muscle is innervated by the trochlear nerve (cranial nerve IV), which controls eye movement, not facial muscles.
 

Option D. Levator palpebrae superioris: This muscle is responsible for elevating the upper eyelid and is innervated by the oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve III).

 

Educational Objective:
 

The Risorius muscle is supplied by the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII), which arises from the brainstem and is responsible for facial expression.

Lateral rectus: This muscle is innervated by the abducens nerve (cranial nerve VI), which is responsible for abducting the eye, not facial expression. Option B. Superior oblique: This muscle is innervated by the trochlear nerve (cranial nerve IV), which controls eye movement, not facial muscles. Option D. questions.stem: The Anesthetist’s artery, a branch of the external carotid artery, is a key vessel responsible for supplying blood to the lower region of the face, including the lips, chin, and cheeks. It courses deep to the submandibular gland, then winds its way along the mandible's lower border, eventually curving up over the mandible at the anteroinferior angle of the masseter muscle. This artery is palpable at the mandibular border and is clinically significant due to its proximity to facial structures and potential involvement in facial surgeries and trauma. Moreover, its pulsation can be an important diagnostic point in physical examinations, particularly in assessing blood flow in the facial region. Which is not a branch of this artery?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Mental


The "Anesthetist's artery" in the question is another name for the facial artery, a key branch of the external carotid artery. The mental artery is not a branch of the facial artery. Instead, it is a branch of the inferior alveolar artery, which itself is a branch of the maxillary artery, another major vessel stemming from the external carotid artery.

 

The facial artery gives rise to multiple branches that supply the facial region:

 

Option A. Lateral nasal artery: Supplies the lateral aspect of the nose.

 

Option C. Superior labial artery: Supplies the upper lip.

 

Option D. Inferior labial artery: Supplies the lower lip.

 

However, the mental artery, which supplies the chin, is derived from the inferior alveolar artery, not directly from the facial artery.

 

Educational Objective:
 

The mental artery is a branch of the inferior alveolar artery, not the facial artery, making it the correct answer as the option that is not a branch of the facial artery.

questions.stem: Which of the following structures passing via the jugular foramen has a separate canal?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Glossopharyngeal nerve


Glossopharyngeal nerve passes via separate sheath through jugular foramen whereas other two nerves - vagus  and accessory nerves pass via common sheath.

 

Other Options:
 

Option A. A) Hypoglossal nerve: The hypoglossal nerve (cranial nerve XII) passes through the hypoglossal canal, which is a separate canal located anterior to the jugular foramen. This nerve is responsible for innervating the muscles of the tongue and plays a key role in controlling tongue movements

 

Option C. Vagus nerve (cranial nerve X): It also passes through the jugular foramen and is responsible for a wide range of functions, including parasympathetic control over many organs.
 

Option D. Accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI): This nerve, which supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles, also exits the skull through the jugular foramen.

 

Educational Objective:
 

Glossopharyngeal nerve, accessory nerve and vagus nerve pass via jugular foramen but glossopharyngeal nerve possesses its own sheath whereas the other nerves have a common sheath.
Hypoglossal nerve passes via hypoglossal canal and not through jugular foramen.

questions.stem: A young man presenting with features of recurrent brief depressive disorder, each lasting for about 3 to 7 days, for over a year. He had a history of occasional headaches and episodes of swooning attacks, usually precipitated by emotional events. His neuroimaging revealed agenesis of the corpus callosum. Recurrent brief depression can be a manifestation of this congenital anomaly, and conversion disorder can be present as a comorbid diagnosis due to ignorance and fear of this malformation. What is the blood supply of the corpus callosum?

options.label: A
options.text: Anterior cerebral artery and middle cerebral artery

options.label: B
options.text: Anterior cerebral artery and posterior cerebral artery

options.label: C
options.text: Anterior cerebral artery and anterior communicating artery

options.label: D
options.text: Middle cerebral artery and posterior cerebral artery

questions.answerText: Anterior cerebral artery and anterior communicating artery
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Anterior cerebral artery and anterior communicating artery


The corpus callosum is primarily supplied by the anterior cerebral artery (ACA), which provides blood to the medial surface of the brain, including most of the corpus callosum. The anterior communicating artery connects the two ACAs, contributing to the blood supply. Together, they ensure sufficient blood flow to the structure. The posterior cerebral artery and middle cerebral artery primarily supply different regions, such as the occipital lobe and lateral brain surfaces, respectively.

 

 

Other Options:
 

Option A. Anterior cerebral artery and middle cerebral artery: The middle cerebral artery does not contribute significantly to the blood supply of the corpus callosum.
 

Option B. Anterior cerebral artery and posterior cerebral artery: The posterior cerebral artery supplies the occipital lobe and posterior regions but does not play a direct role in supplying the corpus callosum.
 

Option D. Middle cerebral artery and posterior cerebral artery: Both of these arteries supply different regions and do not provide blood to the corpus callosum.

 

Educational Objective:
 

The anterior cerebral artery (ACA) and anterior communicating artery are responsible for the blood supply to the corpus callosum, making them critical for maintaining its function.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old male presents to the orthopedic clinic with persistent discomfort and swelling in his right knee. He reports a history of recurrent pain and limited knee movement that worsens during prolonged periods of walking or climbing stairs. On examination, there is tenderness and swelling noted at the posterior aspect of the right knee joint, particularly on the lateral side. Which structure's potential presence, resembling a sesamoid bone, might contribute to the observed discomfort and swelling in the posterior aspect of this patient's right knee?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Lateral head of gastrocnemius


The discomfort and swelling on the lateral side of the posterior knee, as described in the case, suggest the involvement of the lateral head of the gastrocnemius muscle. The presence of the fabella, a sesamoid bone sometimes found within the lateral head of the gastrocnemius tendon, can cause pain and swelling in this region. The fabella can become symptomatic due to mechanical stress during activities such as walking and climbing stairs, leading to irritation, swelling, and discomfort.

 

Other Options:
 

Option A. Medial head of gastrocnemius: Although the gastrocnemius has two heads, the medial head is not typically associated with the fabella, which is more often found in the lateral head.
 

Option C. Adductor magnus: This muscle is located in the medial 

compartment of the thigh and is not involved in the posterior knee region.
Option D. Adductor longus: This muscle is also located in the medial compartment of the thigh and does not contribute to knee joint movements or posterior knee discomfort.

 

Educational Objective:
 

The fabella, a sesamoid bone in the lateral head of the gastrocnemius, may contribute to discomfort and swelling in the posterior lateral knee, particularly during weight-bearing activities.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old lady, Janki, presented with loss of subconscious kinaesthetic sensation, loss of pain and temperature sensation, as well as loss of crude touch from the body. On examination, fine touch sensation was found normal. In the case of spinal angiography, blockage of which of the following arteries might be seen?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Anterior spinal artery


The symptoms described—loss of subconscious kinaesthetic sensation, pain and temperature sensation, and crude touch—suggest involvement of the anterior spinal artery. This artery supplies the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord, which includes structures such as the spinothalamic tract (responsible for pain and temperature sensation) and the ventral spinocerebellar tracts (involved in subconscious kinaesthetic sensation). Since fine touch (carried by the dorsal columns, supplied by the posterior spinal artery) is normal, the pathology is localized to the anterior portion of the spinal cord, which is supplied by the anterior spinal artery.

 

Other Options:


Option B. Posterior spinal artery: This artery supplies the posterior one-third of the spinal cord, including the dorsal columns that are involved in fine touch and proprioception. Since fine touch is preserved, this artery is not implicated.


Option C. Anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA): This artery supplies parts of the cerebellum and brainstem but does not directly supply the spinal cord.


Option D. Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA): Like AICA, PICA supplies parts of the cerebellum and brainstem, not the spinal cord.

 

Educational Objective:


Blockage of the anterior spinal artery results in loss of pain, temperature, crude touch, and kinaesthetic sensation, while preserving fine touch due to the unaffected posterior spinal artery.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old female, Vimla, presented with a road traffic accident and brief loss of consciousness. She was also experiencing fatigue, pallor, weakness, mild jaundice, and gallstones. Massive hepatosplenomegaly and hypersplenism were found. She had a history of failure to thrive, growth retardation, and delayed puberty. After the accident, she is now experiencing headache, a lucid interval, nausea, vomiting, and focal neurological deficits. A skull fracture is visible on plain X-ray, and a hyperdense biconvex opacity is seen on the CT scan in the temporal region. What is your single best diagnosis for her current presentation?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Extradural hemorrhage


The patient's clinical presentation of a head injury with a lucid interval, followed by nausea, vomiting, focal neurological deficits, and the finding of a hyperdense biconvex opacity on the CT scan is characteristic of an extradural hemorrhage (EDH). This type of hemorrhage typically occurs after trauma, particularly involving fractures of the skull, and leads to the accumulation of blood between the skull and dura mater, forming a biconvex hematoma.

 

Her history of thalassemia, causing hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, and gallstones, is important for her overall health but does not explain her acute neurological symptoms post-trauma. Therefore, while her chronic condition is relevant, her current presentation is most consistent with an extradural hemorrhage.

 

Other Options:
 

Option A. Thalassemia: Although the patient has underlying thalassemia, causing hepatosplenomegaly and jaundice, this is not related to her current head trauma symptoms.
 

Option B. Migraine: Migraine is characterized by recurrent headache but does not involve skull fractures, lucid intervals, or CT findings of biconvex hematoma.
 

Option C. Subarachnoid hemorrhage: While this condition can cause a severe headache, it typically presents with a "thunderclap" headache, and the CT findings would show blood in the subarachnoid space rather than a biconvex hematoma.

 

Educational Objective:
 

A lucid interval, followed by neurological deterioration and a biconvex hyperdense lesion on a CT scan, is characteristic of an extradural hemorrhage after head trauma.

questions.stem: A Patient Ramlal, 56 years old male, presented with a history of palanaesthesia, astereognosis, loss of proprioception, and fine touch sensation. He has a chronic history of smoking, diabetes, and hypertension. In the case of spinal angiography, blockage of which of the following arteries might be seen?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Posterior spinal artery


The patient's symptoms—loss of proprioception, astereognosis, palanaesthesia, and fine touch sensation—suggest involvement of the dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus), which carry fine touch, vibration, and proprioception signals. 

 

Spinal cord is supplied by anterior and posterior spinal arteries. Posterior spinal arteries  are responsible for the blood supply of the posterior column of the spinal cord where fasciculus cuneatus and gracilis run. Deficiency or interruption of blood supply will lead to palsy of the nerve fibers running in these columns

 

A blockage in the posterior spinal artery leads to deficits in proprioception and fine touch, while pain and temperature sensations, typically carried by the spinothalamic tract, remain unaffected. This matches the patient's presentation.

 

Other Options:
 

Option A. Anterior spinal artery: The anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord, including the spinothalamic tracts (pain and temperature) and motor tracts, but not the dorsal columns.
 

Option C. Anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA): AICA supplies parts of the brainstem and cerebellum, not the spinal cord.
 

Option D. Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA): PICA supplies the cerebellum and medulla, not the spinal cord.

 

Educational Objective:
 

Blockage of the posterior spinal artery can cause loss of proprioception, fine touch, and vibration, as these sensations are carried by the dorsal columns, which are supplied by this artery.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old male, Jagan, presented with severe headache and vomiting with a history of immediate unconsciousness. On admission, he was found hypertensive, with a history of poorly controlled hypertension. There was a gradual decline in his neurological functions. Neck stiffness and Kernig’s sign were also positive. An NCCT scan failed to make a diagnosis, but a lumbar puncture (LP) revealed grossly bloody cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with RBC counts up to 1 million/cu mm. After 48 hours, xanthochromic spinal fluid was observed. What is your single best diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Subarachnoid hemorrhage


The patient's presentation of a severe headache, immediate unconsciousness, neck stiffness, positive Kernig's sign, and grossly bloody CSF after a lumbar puncture strongly indicates subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). The xanthochromic CSF found 48 hours after the initial presentation is a hallmark of SAH, caused by the breakdown of red blood cells in the CSF, giving it a yellowish appearance. This condition is often related to the rupture of an intracranial aneurysm, frequently linked to poorly controlled hypertension, as seen in this case.

 

Other Options:
 

Option A. Meningitis: While meningitis can cause neck stiffness and positive Kernig's sign, it is not typically associated with grossly bloody CSF.
 

Option B. Intracerebral hemorrhage: This would present with symptoms of a stroke but would not typically cause bloody CSF or xanthochromia.
 

Option D. Extradural hemorrhage: This condition usually presents with a lucid interval followed by a decline in consciousness, but it would not lead to bloody CSF or xanthochromia.

 

Educational Objective:
 

A subarachnoid hemorrhage often presents with a sudden severe headache ("thunderclap headache"), bloody CSF, and xanthochromia after 48 hours, typically following the rupture of an aneurysm.

questions.stem: In adults, lumbar puncture is done at:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) L3 -L4 

 

In adults, a lumbar puncture is performed at the L3-L4 intervertebral space. This location is chosen to avoid injury, which ends at the L1-L2 level in adults. By accessing below this point, the risk of damaging the spinal cord is minimized while safely obtaining cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).

 

Note -  There is controversy regarding the level of spinal puncture. Some authors mention that it is performed at L4-L5 level but anatomy books mention L3-L4 level If L3-L4 is not given in the options then L4-L5 should be chosen

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. L1-L2:
This level is too high for lumbar puncture in adults as the spinal cord is still present here, increasing the risk of injury.

 

Option B. L2-L3:
This is bordering the termination of the spinal cord and is generally avoided for lumbar puncture in adults for safety reasons.

 

Option D. L4-L5:
This is an acceptable alternative site lower than L3-L4 and also considered safe for lumbar puncture, but L3-L4 is the most common preferred level.

 

Educational Objective:


In adults, lumbar puncture is safely performed at the L3-L4 interspace to avoid injury to the spinal cord.

 

Reference - Textbook of clinical Neuroanatomy by Dr. Vishram Singh. Third edition pg54.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old alcoholic and chronic smoker male Amit was having a history of hypercholesterolemia for 8 years. He presented at OPD with hemiplegia on the right side of the body. On examination, he was having loss of proprioception, fine touch, and vibration sensations on the right side. He was also unable to recognize objects with closed eyes from the right hand. On examination, the left side of the tongue was atrophied and deviated to the left side during protrusion. On cerebral angiography, there was blockage of an artery located in the median fissure of the spinal cord at the lower part of the brainstem. What is your diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Dejerine’s syndrome


Dejerine’s syndrome, also known as medial medullary syndrome, occurs when there is a blockage of the anterior spinal artery, affecting the medial part of the medulla. The blockage impacts the pyramidal tract, medial lemniscus, and hypoglossal nerve (cranial nerve XII).

 

In this case, the patient's right-sided hemiplegia, loss of proprioception, fine touch, and vibration, along with left-sided tongue atrophy and deviation, are classic signs of medial medullary syndrome. The hypoglossal nerve involvement leads to ipsilateral tongue atrophy and deviation to the affected side, while the contralateral loss of motor control (hemiplegia) and sensory deficits (proprioception, vibration) are due to damage to the pyramidal tract and medial lemniscus.

 

Other Options:
 

Option A. Perinaud’s syndrome:  It is defined as a group of symptoms which occur due to compression of superior colliculus of midbrain.  Commonly it occurs because of tumours of pineal gland which compress the superior colliculus. MAin clinical feature is loss of upward gaze.
 

Option B. Benedikt’s syndrome: This syndrome involves the midbrain and affects the red nucleus and third nerve, resulting in contralateral tremor and ipsilateral oculomotor palsy, which are not seen in this case.
 

Option D. Wallenberg syndrome: It is lateral medullary syndrome caused due to thrombosis of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery. Symptoms include 

  1. Involvement of spinothalamic tract - Contralateral loss of pain and temperature
  2. Involvement of spinal nucleus and tract of trigeminal - Ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature over face.
  3. Involvement of nucleus ambigus - Ipsilateral loss of motor supply to muscle of pharynx, larynx and palate.
  4. Involvement of inferior cerebellar peduncle - Ataxia (Ipsilateral)
  5. Involvement of reticular formation - horner syndrome.
     

 

Educational Objective:
 

Dejerine’s syndrome (medial medullary syndrome) results from blockage of the anterior spinal artery, affecting the medial medulla, leading to contralateral hemiplegia, sensory deficits, and ipsilateral tongue deviation.

The image shows the 3rd part of the duodenum. The C-loop of the duodenum, as seen in the image, wraps around the head of the pancreas. The duodenum is divided into four parts:
